title: We cannot but speak (Acts 4:13–20)
hook: ordinary uneducated men astonish the council

segments.voice: Yesterday, the man at the Beautiful gate, and silver and gold I have none. Your line was what I have I give. Who did you really look at? Day five hundred thirty-eight.

A diploma on the wall tells you where someone studied. It can't tell you what they've seen. After the healing at the gate, Peter and John spent the night in custody. In the morning they're brought before the council: rulers, elders and scribes, men trained in the law of Moses. Facing them, two fishermen from Galilee. And next to the fishermen, on his own two feet, stands the man who used to beg at the gate. The council has a question for them.
screen: `A DIPLOMA ON THE WALL.` → `A NIGHT IN CUSTODY.` → `THE HEALED MAN STANDS WITH THEM.`

segments.voice: The council asks, by what power, by what name, have you done this? Peter answers: by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth. And then Luke describes the council's reaction. They saw the boldness of Peter and John, and realized they were unlettered, ordinary men, and they were amazed, and they recognized that these two had been with Jesus. Two words in the Greek are worth knowing. Agrammatoi: unlettered, not trained in the schools of the law. And idiōtai: ordinary people, private persons, not officials. English later got the word idiot from it, but here it just means laymen. The Douay calls their courage constancy. The Greek is parrēsia, freedom of speech, the boldness to say everything plainly. And the council can't say much back, Luke notes, because the healed man is standing right there. So they order the two to stop speaking or teaching in the name of Jesus at all. Peter and John answer: whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you judge. And then, in the Douay-Rheims: "For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard." Notice, it's not stubbornness, and it isn't a debating point. They simply can't un-see what they saw. It's the word from four days ago, witness, under pressure. And the reason given for their boldness isn't schooling. It's that they had been with Jesus. Catholics see the same pattern in some saints with little schooling. Catherine of Siena, tradition says, learned to write only late in life, and the Church later named her a Doctor of the Church.
screen: `BY WHAT NAME?` · `UNLETTERED, ORDINARY MEN.` · `THEY HAD BEEN WITH JESUS.` · `WHAT WE HAVE SEEN AND HEARD.` · then, large: `WE CANNOT BUT SPEAK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember what you've seen. Sit and breathe. Let your mind go back to one thing you've witnessed yourself that you can't un-see: an act of kindness that stopped you, a recovery, a forgiveness, a moment in prayer, something beautiful. Not something you read. Something you saw or heard. Let the details come back. Then think of who might need to hear about it. If you pray, you can give thanks for it, and hold the line, we cannot but speak. If you don't, just hold the memory. The bell holds the time.
Parrēsia. The Greek word for the boldness of two unlettered fishermen before the council, the courage that came from having been with Jesus. Today's word.
Your line: they had been with Jesus. Today, tell someone about something you've seen or experienced, plainly, without dressing it up. Day five hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics read the Acts of the Apostles at Mass through the Easter season, and the Church keeps a feast for Catherine of Siena, a Doctor of the Church with little formal schooling.

original.note: Greek: boldness, frankness, saying everything (Acts 4:13). The Douay has constancy.

trapdoor: what you thought: brave men defying authority.
what it means: ordinary people who can't un-see what they saw, and whose boldness comes from having been with Jesus.
what a scholar hears: agrammatoi and idiōtai mean untrained and lay, not illiterate fools; parrēsia, frank speech, becomes a key word in Acts (4:13, 29, 31).
